To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the risk of developing TB disease among persons who are HIV-positive and who are infected with M tuberculosis is high; 2) preventive therapy with isoniazid is effective in reducing this risk; and 3) isoniazid should be used as a component of TB prevention in HIV-positive patients.

TB preventive therapy is an important intervention that should be incorporated into the care of HIVinfected persons and that research on the implementation of TB preventive therapy should be a high priority.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevention of TB in HIV-infected individuals.
the development and evaluation of new methods to control and eliminate TB in the developing world, and the development of novel vaccines against TB.
the development and application of new methods of diagnosis, prevention and treatment of tuberculosis (TB), with the ultimate aim of reducing the incidence and severity of this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TB preventive therapy is an important and cost-effective intervention that should be incorporated into the routine care of HIV-inflicted persons.
TB preventive therapy should be provided for all HIV-infected persons in whom active TB has been excluded.
TB preventive therapy is indicated in HIV-infected persons with a positive tuberculin skin test result or a positive interferon-gamma release assay result.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have a lot of work to do in order to improve the quality of TB treatment and prevention in the era of AIDS.
the HIV epidemic has led to renewed attention to the problem of TB, which is now a major cause of death among HIV-infected persons in many areas of the world.

the use of TB preventive therapy for HIV-infected persons should be based on the following considerations: the presence of a positive tuberculin skin test, the presence of a high-risk clinical condition for the development of active TB (eg, HIV infection), and the absence of active TB.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current state of TB preventive therapy is not satisfactory, but that the tools are available to improve this situation.

TB prevention in HIV-infected individuals is a critical public health priority, and that the current research agenda should be expanded to include studies of the optimal duration of TB preventive therapy for HIV-infected individuals and of the role of such therapy in the treatment and prevention of TB in HIV-infected persons receiving antiretrovirals.

we need to develop a better understanding of the epidemiology of latent TB infection (LTBI) and TB in HIV-infected persons, including the risk factors for progression of LTBI to TB disease and the impact of HIV on the pathogenesis and clinical manifestations of TB.
